notes: \cpara{Opens with a question: is a robin or an ostrich the more typical bird?}
\cpara{Asks the same question about three kinds of chair.}

\cpara{Introduces typicality effects. The verification-time finding is reported as the cited volume reports it: in such tasks, responses of ``true'' ``are invariably faster for the items that have been rated more prototypical'' (Rosch, ``Principles of Categorization,'' 1978). The post is unsure of its own source (``reasonably sure''), but the finding does not depend on it.}
\cpara{Asks whether typicality, which may work as a heuristic, has a matching bias that would show it at work.}

\cpara{Gives two asymmetries. The country result matches Tversky and Gati's table: Mexico was rated 7.65 in similarity to the United States, and the United States 6.46 in similarity to Mexico, on a scale of 1 to 20. Across their 21 pairs of countries the average difference was 0.42 points, statistically significant, and six pairs went the other way. The asymmetry is real and small.}

\cfact{The comparison is not in the cited paper, which I read in full (pp.~430--439). Sadock gives a theory of when an approximation counts as true, and reports no test of what most people prefer here. The paper's nearest point supports the post: a round figure sets a coarser scale, so ``approximately one million'' can be a better approximation than ``approximately 990,000.'' The experimental evidence is Rosch's (1975): given frames such as ``X is virtually Y,'' subjects ``reliably placed the more prototypical member of a pair of items into the referent slot'' (Rosch 1978), and the items included round and non-round numbers.}

\cpara{Reports Rips's study of induction and argues that the asymmetry has no practical basis. I could not read the paper. Heit's review (2000) confirms the design, a ``new type of contagious disease'' found on ``a small island,'' and the direction of the effect, with other birds: a bluejay premise ``led to stronger inferences overall than did having goose.'' I could not check whether robins and ducks were among the species.}

\clogic{Stated as a fact about what is reasonable, and disputed. Heit's Bayesian model (1998), offered as an analysis of ``what, given certain assumptions, would be normative,'' predicts this asymmetry. It assumes that atypical species are believed to have many features of their own, so that a new property of one ``would suggest that this property is likewise idiosyncratic and not to be widely projected'' (Heit 2000). Whether Rips's subjects reasoned this way is a separate question, which the next paragraph raises.}
\cpara{Warns against rationalizing the subjects' answers, and offers the simpler explanation: people use similarity, which is asymmetric, as a stand-in for the probability of spread.}

\clogic{This is the post's interpretation, not the study's. Rips measured similarity as distance in a scaling solution, which is symmetric, and found a separate effect of the premise species' typicality: ``Rips (1975) found distinct contributions of premise--conclusion similarity and premise typicality'' (Heit 2000). Of the same asymmetry in later experiments, Heit writes that it ``follows from the premise typicality effect.'' An asymmetric similarity, in the manner of Tversky, is a possible alternative, but the study does not show it. Both accounts give typicality the central role.}

\cpara{Gives a spatial version: people seem to treat closeness as a property of Kansas and distance as a property of Alaska. The post offers it with ``seem'' and no study. There is one: Sadalla, Burroughs and Staplin (1980) found that ``The subjective distance between reference points and nonreference points was found to be asymmetrical.''}
\cpara{Draws the conclusion: the Aristotelian model of categories fails, and people treat membership as a matter of degree.}

\clogic{The evidence in the post is typicality, and typicality does not show graded membership. Armstrong, Gleitman and Gleitman (1983) found typicality gradients for categories with exact definitions: ``some odd numbers (e.g., 3) are judged as being more typical than other odd numbers (e.g., 4,284,647).'' Rips, whose study the post cites, concludes with a coauthor that ``typicality gradients are not diagnostic of a category's lack of precise definition'' (Rips and Thompson, 2014). Membership may still be graded for some categories; this post does not show it.}
\cpara{Closes with a link back to ``Words as Hidden Inferences'': one more reason not to pretend that anyone treats words as Aristotelian classes.}
